Honestly, I was originally going to give Rogue Core a good 10 hours before making a review for it, but I just can't force myself through the drudgery that is Rogue Core's overly stripped down missions. I expected a lot better from the devs as Ghost Ship Games.

And I'm sorry if this review becomes kind of long, but I have a lot to say, so please bear with me.


And this is to the devs at Ghost Ship Games specifically. 

If you guys can't handle criticism from users, then I will just say this to you guys.

Either learn to maturely take and act upon fans' criticism like adults or get the hell out of the gaming market and go do something else! Because you are [b]NOT[/b] entitled to success nor are you free from criticism just because you're a smaller game studio!

I don't care if that sounds rather harsh, I'm no one's yes man nor will I give any devs a completely free pass without some damn good reasons for it. I refuse to only tell people what they [b]want[/b] to hear, and these guys need to actually listen to fans and not get on any kind of high horses and fight with their fans or whatever.

Don't be like the stupid higher ups at companies like EA, Blizzard, or Activision who just do stupid things that come back to bite them. I don't think you guys are like that, but don't start down such a path.


But honestly, the GSG devs [b]SHOULD'VE[/b] made Rogue Core a proper DRG2 to solidify the DRG series instead of trying to go off and make a spinoff game like this. 

And I for one think most of us would've probably been fine with the GSG devs taking current DRG and copy and pasting its data and using it as the foundation for building upon that to make a proper DRG2, but with many new additions of course.

But Rogue Core isn't a truly horrible game by any means, but it feels like a giant mess of a game none the less, like the GSG devs wanted to just make a roguelike FPS game, but then decided they had to tie it in with Deep Rock Galactic, and hence we have this messy game.

I probably would've liked this game more if the devs really worked to either go a bit further with making the game more of a roguelike/lite game, with no classes but maybe some skill trees that allow players to choose a bunch of different generalized roles, or, like I said, make the classes far more distinct like in DRG, but with a few new classes as well, because the classes in Rogue Core feel very lackluster and like major downgrades from the ones in DRG.

But honestly, game feels incredibly underwhelming because of how the roguelite elements seem to work against the fun aspects of a co-op shooter game like DRG, like how there are no persistent loadouts to drop into a mission with, it feels like there's no point to even trying to choose different playstyles, as it's all just random nonsense.

And as many have already said. That damn mission timer [b]has[/b] to be removed as a fixture of all missions.

If it was a little longer and only as a type of difficulty option to select for a Lethal+ level of difficulty, that'd be one thing, but it feels like it goes by so damn quickly that's it feels oppressive rather than actually adding any kind of legit challenge to the game.

But I think that the GSG devs should not try to keep Rogue Core bound to all the bog standard roguelike stuff, like random missions and weapons and so on, but try to break the mold and add in some elements that are not only different but could potentially still work within a roguelite game.

I could see a Weapon Forging mechanic for either Rogue Core or a possible future DRG2 where you can essentially forge your own upgraded versions of the different types of weapons in the game and drop into missions with them, but there's an element of risk to it.

I would say that the risk for such a possible mechanic could easily be that there's a chance to lose such powerful custom weapons if you fail a mission, so it could become a bit of a meta game of sorts where you weigh bringing powerful custom weapons with you or not.

But I honestly think that Rogue Core has plenty of potential, but the devs seriously [b]NEED[/b] to listen to fans and not just try to stubbornly stick to keeping the game as overly restrictive as it currently is.

Rogue Core isn't as bad as many of the reviews claim, a lot of them having severe rose-tinted glasses for DRG or just not vibing with roguelikes. I have already racked up half of my total playtime of Risk of Rain 2 in Rogue Core and I enjoy playing Rogue Core co-op with a friend more than I did with RoR2 (that game is barely co-op to begin with and is better played solo). When DRG dropped into early access it was in a much rougher state than Rogue Core, with years of updates and feedback needed to bring it to the state it is in today. Rogue Core is already very polished for a early access release and has a gameplay loop that offers several hours of gameplay. I'm a huge DRG fan that has extracted thousands of hours of enjoyment from DRG and I believe Rogue Core will be the same story. But the game still needs more work, changes and updated to get to that point.

- The timer doesn't take into account complexity. You have as much time on your hands on Complexity 1 as you do on Complexity 3. Having an additional multiplier that gives you a little more time depending on the complexity level could help. The player count time multiplier could do with a 3% increase as well.
- There is a severe time-and-effort discrepancy between Expenite Events. Cargo Hauling takes little time and effort to complete, paying out the same amount of Expenite as the Ram Hammer Escort. The Research Subject event can either be a breeze to do, or be the worst slog in the world that can pay out much less than every other event depending on if you have the ability to freeze it or not. There needs to be some balancing to make the slow, tedious and risky events feel worth doing compared to the significantly less hazardous events.
- Too many filler upgrades. There are some really good upgrades buried under a trash heap of upgrades that really need QoL and additional minor effects. It feels bad to get melee upgrades when you aren't playing Slicer or have the drills. Giving some upgrades a minor bonus effect that synergize with itself would help make them more interesting. Why not give Combo Strike a +5% increase to swing speed, Nerves Of Steel +10% recoil reduction, Critical Strike gives your pickaxe +4% crit chance.
- Not enough elemental upgrades and terrible synergy between the elements. Fire and Ice have temperature shock and are very strong on their own, plus they are the easiest to build into as you very often get the Incendiary grenade and the Cryo grenade at the start. Electricity no longer procs like in DRG, requiring you to build it up like you do with Fire and Ice. Radiation is strong if you get it on a weapon with AoE but it has no elemental synergy to speak of and not a single upgrade to make a build out of it. Poison and Acid are bad, with Poison only having 4 rather bad upgrades and Acid having none. Any element that isn't Fire or Ice have terrible synergies with each other, are too conditional to be useful, and have pretty bad payoffs for even procing them.
-There aren't enough unique weapon upgrades and some weapons have so many upgrades that you have a low chance of getting something useful. I had two workbenches where the upgrades were both of the times Rate of Fire and Recoil Control for the Stubby SMG. Some upgrades could honestly be combined with each other to reduce the clutter. Imagine getting the choice between having Shot Spread + Weak-point Damage and Rate of Fire + Damage. Upping the selection from 2 weapon upgrades to 3 could alleviate some of the issues of getting weapon upgrades you don't want. That or a re-roll option. More weapons need unique upgrades and some of existing are underwhelming or outright terrible. I'm looking at you Decker with your Bleed Bullets.
- Enemy balance. The Corespawn are much more durable, agile and deadlier than the Glyphids, making Rogue Core much more challenging compared DRG. I'm fine with the enemies being much more challenging than the Glyphids in DRG but making them into bulletsponges doesn't make it a interesting one. What the Corespawn lack is distinct niche they are try to fill and weaknesses to compensate for their strengths. In DRG the enemies followed some kind of archetype and are balanced around it. The Glyphid Guard is more durable and armored compared to the regular Grunt, but move much slower if they get shot at and spawn in lesser numbers. The Corespawn Vanguard on the other hand have double the health of a Creeper, deals more damage, move much faster and is just a complete nuisance with how many the game throws at you. The Bruiser is not only super durable and deal a severe amount of damage but they can also knock you back. None of the enemies have specific damage types that they are weak to, no additional weak-points to exploit or interesting ways to counter them.

Beyond those issues I have only a few minor nitpicks.
- The old DRG weapons are much less detailed than the Rogue Core weapons and could do with a re-model or update to bring them up to par.
- The Enhancement selection in the loadout menu becomes very cluttered after you have unlocked every tier. A suggestion I have is that when you unlock a new tier, it should hide the previous one and only display a lower tier Enhancement if you have already slotted in the highest version. There is no reason for us to be able to select Tier 1 of Skull Crusher when you already Tier 4 unlocked and ready to be used.
- Some of the doors in missions take too long to open and close, plus they don't stay open for long to kick the bucket of Expenite and leave.
- The game spawns most of the armor pickups in the starting cave of the next level instead of spreading it throughout the cave.
- The sound of the Pickaxe Customization Terminal is becoming grating from passing it by to get to the Ascension hall or going to the Wardrobe Terminal.
The game has a solid foundation but needs more work for it to become a truly great co-op roguelike experience where working with your team matters.

Every gun feels terrible to use, only a few are somewhat decent after you upgrade it. I don't necessarily mean their strength but the gunplay in general feels bad. It's like the game was made with ADS in mind but never actually implemented it, so you're stuck with an inconsistent feeling hipfire profile for everything that feels like it has an identity crisis.

So if the game doesn't really want the guns to be the focus, then maybe the abilities of the characters are the main combat incentive... Nope, your abilities have long cooldown times, effects that last a very short amount of time, and that feel nearly decoupled from the character as a whole. The power of the abilities is also fine here, much like the damage output of the guns. The difficulty / damage of this game isn't the main problem, it's that it feels like the game is created in a way that makes everything inconvenient to use and clunky.

The boss fights are uninspired copy pastes of eachother with minor differences between the actual boss mechanics. The bosses themselves are huge bullet sponges and the game doesn't provide you with enough ammo to kill them in half of the runs, so you end up needing to backtrack through the cave to find an ammo drop that you didn't already collect, all while the boss ignores the cave walls and snipes you while clipping through the environment. It doesn't carve holes where it went, doesn't blast open the caves as it trudges through rock, just phases through until it does a move that locks you in where you can't do anything but take the damage and wait to die.

The start of each run has an entirely unnecessary time bloating entrance sequence where you activate two robots and run through a small cave into a room where you pick up your weapon and grenade for the start of the run, nothing too egregious here, but it wastes a lot of time for something that could have been implemented on the drop pod you get sent into the mission on to the same effect while saving all of that time.

You are playing a cooperative game that has you competing against your allies for perks where the person choosing first is randomly selected and then rotated for every pickup after that. This can often cause one person to get completely shafted on their drops because people take the strongest perks first, and when it's your time to pick, the whole table rolls commons. So not only are you limited in the quantity of pickups in a single run, but you have to double roll on RNG to even get useful items and also in a way where you can actually pick them.

The character upgrade tree seems quite expansive at first, until you realize that this huge tree you're grabbing is actually just selectable perks that you can slot into 8 slots that you unlock per character, you do not gain the effect of the whole tree. This isn't necessarily a problem, but does lead to the fact that these early bonuses are almost entirely unnoticeable on your character. Sprinting for a few seconds to gain a 5% sprint speed boost is not useful in the slightest. So you're stuck feeling like the worst version of the character until you reach the end of the entire tree to be able to select a perk that may have a 15% effect on one aspect of your character.

In general, I'm enjoying DRG Rogue Core a lot.
That's the short answer, i still have a longer answer and some complaints:

DRG Rogue Core is not completely "DRG 2", and that's fine, I am a worm timer defender, and it was already a thing in Base DRG with swarms getting bigger and bigger until a dreadnought spawns, but it never goes noticed unless you spend 3 hours in a cave with other players because it's wayyy more lenient then Rogue Core's worm timer.

HOWEVER, in terms of minute-to-minute gameplay mechanics, i would prefer if more base DRG players would occupy the public population of this game, because I've had too many games with randoms who presumably haven't played base DRG, where people:

1: rush side objectives or stack swarms while their team has no ammo or time.
2: don't listen to their team, level/upgrade dibs, Ctrl+RMB pings, the text chat, OR the voice chat.
3: Don't understand basic DRG gameplay mechanics, like movement tools (drills, plats, ziplines, etc) or how to use their abilities in general.

If you're reading this and you haven't played Base DRG, I BEG you, PLEASE. for the LOVE of GOODNESS GRACIOUS: try the base game, spend at least more than 10 minutes as a class that isn't gunner (preferably driller or scout) and give Rogue Core a different point of view. 
it goes on sale very often and is much more polished than Rogue Core currently.

I could complain about the game itself being difficult, or it's conflicting game mechanics, and I will.
But if you know anything about Base DRG, you know how annoying it is when someone isn't doing their part, and the randoms/public lobby experience bothers me more than the actual gameplay.

WHINING ASIDE, ACTUAL GAMEPLAY STUFF:

The difficulty curve feels very sudden and steep with the depth mechanic, which isn't the biggest problem, my main gripe is that just like in, you guessed it, Base DRG: the difficulty is increased or decreased not only with more or less enemy spawns but also with more or less special enemies.
This bothers me in particular in Base DRG because if i want to bring over friends who aren't used to FPS'es to the game, say on a lower Haz mission, they'll see less different types of enemies and be less prepared or knowledgeable for higher and higher hazard missions on their own.
Rogue Core's enemy designs exacerbate this issue by being more powerful or more annoying in general, and even if they didn't: picking between a mission with only 4 to 5 enemy types or a mission that overwhelms you with all of the available enemy types is just not very good design in both games.

- Lack of variety (the game desperately needs more grenade options and enemy types)
- Unfair difficulty (sometimes enemies clip through walls, making them impossible to counter)
- Boring meta-progression (mostly just flat stat increases with nothing that opens up new build potential)

Frankly, I think people are just averse to the difficulty, particularly because the missions become quite challenging as soon as you hit Depth 2, which doesn't take long. Hey heads up reader - this game is in early access, its a roguelite, and you have to work together as a team. That should address the concerns of 75% of the negative reviews.

So far I love what I'm seeing from this game. The timer on missions really pushes your team to prioritize making it safely to the next level vs. finding more expenite for that next upgrade, with enough variables going on that the decision is not always the same. Sometimes it is worth staying longer, and sometimes its not. 

Personally I like the upgrade system, having to get everyone together and then choosing from the same set of upgrades. Hot tip, you don't have to upgrade as soon as it available. You can just keep moving along and not have to worry about getting everyone together for a single upgrade. Save until the elevator and get 4 at once, which gives you more time to find more expenite to get to those 4. 

I've done solo runs, duos with a friend, and quads with randoms - and with friends or randoms is where it really shines. Making decisions as a team, letting others have an upgrade that will go better with their build instead of yours, staying on the move, and ammo management is what this game is all about. [b]Прежде всего:[/b] если думали, что это DRG2 - идём мимо, не задерживаемся. Реюз контента и общий сеттинг - это всё, что роднит данный вбоквел с основной игрой. Убрать всё визуально знакомое, дать другое название и никакого родства не останется. Для тех, кого это не смущает - продолжим.

[h1]Беги, Споттер, беги![/h1]

Первый ключевой момент игры и, по совместительству, основная боль ищущих DRG2 - таймер. Этот надоедливый ромбик в левом верхнем игру с утекающей полоской постоянно действует на нервы, не давая обслюнявить каждый сантиметр пещеры. Чем выше сложность и комплексность генерации - тем чаще встаёт выбор между уйти сейчас или рискнуть и сделать ещё один ивент ради потенциально хорошего апгрейда. При этом сам по себе таймер не убивает, но когда время кончается - местные космические макаки начинают валить из разломов без остановки. Но самое главное - черви. Бессмертные черви, хватающие дворфов и утаскивающие их на следующий этаж, если вовремя не шугнуть свинцом.

По началу бесит неимоверно. Потом осваиваешься. Понимаешь, что движение - жизнь. В итоге приходит осознание, что без таймера игра бы просто не работала. Тебе нужен этот стимул, этот уровень принятия решений. Тем более, что остальной дизайн игры с ним вполне сочетается. Здесь есть всего один ресурс для добычи и всего несколько точек интереса на каждом этаже помимо него при том, что основная задача всегда одинаковая - добраться до лифта, уехать ниже, в самом низу завалить большую ебаку. Одну из трёх, пока что.

Да и, честно говоря, полный забег и с таймером-то идёт от 30 до 70 минут, в зависимости от вашей скорости и количества этажей.

[h1]Кто первый встал - того и пушка...[/h1]

Отряд спускается в пещеру без нихрена. По какой в точности причине, кроме описанной чуть позже, у вас нет хотя бы одной фиксированной стартовой пушки - не ясно. Вооружаемся в первой комнате.

И тут видим второй ключевой момент игры и самую спорную его часть - общий пул выбора на всю команду. Как это выглядит: подходим в круг, игра ставится на паузу и вам предлагают несколько вариантов из которых в порядке очереди каждый из отряда выбирает что-то одно и следующий выбранное взять уже не может, выбирая из того, что осталось. Это осознанное дизайнерское решение. Такое же, как необходимость всему отряду собираться в кругах, для активации выбора.

Звучит ужасно. В половине случаев делает игру с рандомами фрустрирующим опытом. В целом же, не так страшно за счёт невозможности нахождения в отряде двух одинаковых классов и невозможности со старта получить одинаковые пушки. Вам не нужны одинаковые апгрейды большую часть времени, даже если очень сильно хочется. Есть, конечно, пачка относительно универсальных штук, которые придутся кстати всегда, но в основном больше бесит не общий пул на команду, а сам ролл выпавшего.

[h1]Все профессии нужны, все профессии - не влезут[/h1]

Дворфов теперь пять, а мест в отряде так же - четыре, при том, что скиллы у ребят отличаются. Очень сильно отличаются. Это означает, что для полной команды есть четыре разные комбинации классов, в каждой из которых чего-то будет не доставать. То патроны резко закончатся, а ящик скинуть некому; то неудачный спавн волны вайпнет всю тиму, а самовоскрешающегося реткона в ней нет; то с апгрейдами на сустейн не повезёт, а маяк с регеном армора остался вместе с гардианом на базе... всякое случается.

При этом у каждого класса кроме скиллов есть свои особые апгрейды - био-бустеры, которые могут значительно изменить ситуацию по ходу забега. Игра даже позволяет менять наборы бустеров между классами, но для этого надо прокачать до упора не только класс кому менять, но и с кого. Это значит, что воспользоваться этой фичей можно минимум после асценда двух разных классов и заменить можно только один набор из двух.

Все пять классов играются хорошо с единственной оговоркой: инпут активации навыков. Часть можно поменять в настройках, но переназначить полностью всю схему игра не даёт.

[h1]Метапрогрессия[/h1]

Мы тут в рогалике, как никак и самое стрёмное, что я могу рассказать по этому поводу - валюта. Она нужна на открытие слотов для перков, на открытие слотов дейликов, на разблокировку тиров перков и на асценд.

Первый способ получения валюты такой же, как в основной игре - за милстоны. Насобирал сколько-то камер в пещере - вот тебе горстка валюты. Убил сколько-то врагов - вот тебе ещё горстка. Милстонов много, но чем дольше ты играешь - тем реже ты получаешь валюту, т.к. трешхолды увеличиваются. Учитывая, что у каждого класса по восемь слотов под перки и сами перки разделены на четыре тира - можно оказаться в ситуации где у тебя полно места под перки, полно чипов для приобретения следующего тира перков, но нихрена нет валюты, чтобы открыть этот тир. Если что, гейт на финальный четвёртый тир - 7500 и это нифига не маленькая сумма. Я же был в обратной ситуации: открыл и загриндил перки четвёртого тира, но мне некуда было их ставить - не хватало валюты для слотов на новых классах. До сих пор не хватает, но шесть слотов вместо двух - уже лучше.

В дальнейшем можно получать валюту с дейликов, а после асценда даётся доступ к испытаниям, где тоже предлагают неплохое количество в награду, если осилить.

Сами перки при этом стоят того, чтобы с этим заморачиваться. Первый тир, ожидаемо, не особо сильный, но добравшись до четвёртого... ух, это весьма значимые цифры и возможности, которые заметно упрощают жизнь в пещере. Чипы на прокачку перков даются просто за опыт в забегах.

При этом у самих пещер тоже есть своя прогрессия. Сейчас она поделена на 8 уровней, в каждом из которых надо выполнять какие-то условия: собирать камеры в указаных биомах, бить боссов, проходить на определённой сложности и т.д. Открываются за это новые биомы, возможность активации новых ивентов, более глубокая сложность, комплексность генерации, больше выбора модификаторов между этажами, глобальные модификаторы забега. В общем, заняться есть чем.

[h1]Разное спорное[/h1]

Мне персонально не нравится механика брони в этой игре. Мало того, что вместо перезаряжающегося энергощита у нас тут конечный ресурс армора, так он ещё и работает как демедж редакшн: пока у тебя есть хотя бы одна единица брони - урон по хп снижен на 50%. Это буквально означает, что иметь какой-то сустейн малого количества армора выгодней, чем разгонять её вместимость.

Часть новых пушек как будто специально сделана так, что ими просто невозможно играть без перков или апгрейдов на снижение отдачи. Там такой бешеный рекоил, что стабильно попадать из этой хреновины - не самая тривиальная задача. Я уж молчу, что попадать надо в уязвимую точку, а не куда-то там. Патроны в дефиците, да и враги порезвее жуков из основной игры.

Френдли фаер весьма брутален в условиях жёсткой нехватки хп и армора при необходимости кучковаться время от времени. Никаких перков, чтобы это нивелировать в игре сейчас нет, хотя вроде как были в альфе, но я сам не видел.

В соло играть легче, чем вдвоём. По тем же причинам, что и в основной игре - Купер, младший братан Боско, слишком хорош. Втроём играть приятнее, чем вчетвером - пул выбора апгрейдов уже как на полную команду, но хаоса и потенциального френдли фаера в замесах происходит не на столько много.

[h1]Так что в итоге?[/h1]

Играбельно. Вполне. Рандом вносит свою перчинку, но тут может быть весело и интересно. Контента маловато и в плане его качества есть куда стремиться, но для раннего доступа - вполне солидно. Не пожалел.

[b]P.S.:[/b] Музыка в игре хороша. Особенно в активных фазах забегов.

It's Elden Ring: Nightreign but with Deep Rock DNA and it friggin' slaps.

+ The classes are all pretty fun to play, and it's hard to pick a favourite. Just when I think one class is mid, I'll give them another shot and I'll end up figuring out how they fit into a team and what cool builds I can put on them.
+ The roguelite elements of making weird builds for each run and adding progression buffs per class make for some improvised creative builds.
+ Femme dwarves, and they have sick beards and mohawks.  Hell yeah
+ I would've been happy with just the weapons from Deep Rock Galactic and Deep Rock Survivor, but the new additions on top of those are creative at worst, and brilliant at best - from a pistol that shoots projectile blocking shields (great for melee classes and for support) to a slow punchy rifle that shoots giant slugs.

- The UI for equipping buffs for each class/loadout quickly gets cluttered and hard to read, with no way to organize it [as of this writing in Early Access, late May]
- Unlocking cosmetics with your "scrips" you earn is done per class, instead of across the board. This makes things a little clunky, having to dig around to double check which class has which beard etc

The more linear cave design and the voice-cues from the narrator help this, design wise. Just be patient with people and yourself. Even failed runs produce progression! Rock and Stone!
= Beer that provides buffs would be cool, but I suspect that'll be added once they figure out how to balance it.

TLDR: It's Nightreign but Deep Rock and I mean it. You're going to be motoring through quickly and risking it for the biscuit. Normally I like waiting out Early Access, but this is worth it right now to get in early!

Really wish Steam had more review options beside "Yes" and "No", but in it's current state, to an overall degree, I cannot recommend this in confidence the way I can with the first DRG.
Rogue Core feels somehow just like DRG, but so different, but it's not the differences that make it unbearable.

If you are a DRG player just looking for more fun "haha dwarf say funny line, oo~ shiny rock, gun do warcrimes" gameplay, this is not it. (you will be told you are a Reclaimer, not a Miner.)
Rogue Core was advertised as "DRG with Roguelite elements"
Rogue Core feels like "players said Haz 5 DRG was too easy" with Roguelite elements.

Many things feel way overtuned against you, and it feels like a constant uphill battle against the timer, ammo economy, and RNG deciding to be merciful on your drops. Alone, all of these things are fine, when combined, they created a tense experience of feeling rushed that just doesn't work.

Rogue Core is obviously designed to be a challenge. You will, of course, not win every single run. However, a game being challenging should be secondary to it being fun. And the challenge this game offers to casual/solo players, is not fun.

Like many reviews state, the game struggles with crowd control despite being a horde shooter. 
The game simply doesn't provide enough tools to manage the number of enemies it throws at you, making Guardian feel less like a build choice and more like a requirement for basic survival.

This issue is amplified by the game's ammo economy. Enemies are highly aggressive and surprisingly durable, even on lower difficulties, yet ammunition remains scarce. 
Because firearms are the player's primary method of dealing with hordes, every encounter eventually becomes a lose-lose situation: stand your ground and burn through precious ammo while enemies swarm from multiple directions, or retreat constantly and spend the mission running from fights instead of engaging with them. (you better love prey animal gameplay)

Rather than feeling challenged, the player often feels deliberately under equipped for the situations the game creates.

All of the things that provide a challenge would be fine alone, but its because they are together, it goes from a fun challenge to an annoying race against RNG that you will probably lose anyways.

I feel DRG does far superior in terms of being accessible to both hardcore players seeking a challenge, and casual/solo players looking for just, well, a casual experience. 

I REALLY hope it's only uphill from here, but unless you are a gaming god or a masochist, I cannot recommend this.

Alright, after quite a few hours and some facilities cleared, I wanted to write an actual review of the good the bad and the ugly here. I'm honestly pretty happy with the game, having a lot of fun with it. You can tell it's EA because there's a huge world of improvements than can be made, but the way it currently is results in a perfectly serviceable 7/10. With more work, I'm confident we'll have another rock and stone certified classic.

THE GOOD

- The core gameplay loop is good. Each facility is entertaining, you never quite know what can go wrong - it's fun and engaging. If you happen across the proper randoms, you can have a lot of fun, but if you don't it's still good. 
- It's easy to jump in and difficult to master. The guiding cable helps a lot in not getting lost and avoiding people ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ around. The classes' abilities are useful and fun but not overly complicated to time. I feel it's more accessible for newcomers than DRG. 
- The classes are distinct enough to matter, but not so critical that the game becomes a slog if one isn't present or its player is not very good. 
- The minigames are fun and in character, the voice actors rock, and the critters are fun and dangerous. 

THE BAD

- The negotiation mechanic is a bit of a flowbreaker, and it certainly needs a reroll mechanic. Too much is at stake in the first selection of weapons to not give the player at least a bit of wiggle room. 
- I don't really have a problem with the timer, but it'd probably be better if the players had a couple extra minutes, and/or a mechanic to gain time. If the Expenite events are a gamble - gain upgrades, lose time, health, ammo - you could do something similar. Close this portal and gain X amount of timer, risk a swarm, or a sentinel, or whatever. It seems relatively easy to give options. Chalk it up to EA.
- The difficulty loop seems good to me, but I'd expand the loadout options a little bit more. You have a lot of perks to choose from, and you're limited to just 6; it works against meaningful synergies, or having your dwarf be the way you want it to be. 

THE UGLY AND THE PRETTY

- I feel the game doesn't really know what it wants to be tone-wise. The operator aesthetic, banter, and general tone of the classes collides a bit with the rather DRG dancing, pickaxe-waving, disapproving Mission Control and such. Give us some more military humor! Make the classes feel like the world-class operators they are supposed to be! Weird dwarf salutes, more 'operator' focused cosmetics, combat knives used as mining implements!
- The soundtrack - especially the jukebox - could really use some more character. Get Wind Rose to crank up some metal!
- The gym minigames rock, and really go with the whole 'l33t operators' vibe. Give us a bit more! A shooting range, an obstacle course! Some more beers, less focused on mining and more on reclaiming!
- While I do miss Mission Control from DRG, Omega seems pretty cool. I'd give it a more synthetic, hyperfocused vibe rather than its current incarnation, but there's a lot of potential.

I love this game! I feel like normally I don't need to write a review to express my enjoyment of a game, but the unrelenting backlash yields mixed feelings online and has deterred people I know from even giving the game a real shot. I think there are a lot of fair and even deserved criticisms that can be levied against Rogue Core in its current state. As an early access game hat is a relatively extreme departure from the original, giving constructive feedback is great for improving the game. This isn't a comprehensive review because there isn't much I can say that hasn't already been said. I love this game and acknowledge its flaws. All I can do is give positive constructive feedback and hope to see more improvements.

The Good:
Each class in the game feels uniquely fun and distinct in a way that has endeared me to each of the Reclaimers. I love the variety of builds the game affords as opposed to the more limited options per class in DRG. The overall faster pace makes runs feel more unique, and each team composition feels a lot more impactful than the original game because of the variety afforded each character. It a lot harder and more unforgiving than the original in a way that just really excites me. I find myself diving into runs more and more as I relish in the difficulty. Beating a run feels very satisfying in a way that no individual DRG run ever really has for me. There is this ramping intensity that grows throughout a dive and it is so satisfying when a build comes together. The large number of objectives on each floor means that your team of dwarves has to decide how you will tackle hitting all your objectives before the timer runs out. There's just so much to enjoy and I am having a blast!

The Bad:
That in mind, I want to encourage people to continually make constructive criticism about things that frustrate them. I understand the difficulties with the timer, the shared upgrade system feeling unfair, and the clunky implementation of the roguelike mechanics in places that clashes with DRGs core mechanics. I think all of these complaints are fair and there is a lot of tweaking that could be done to improve the core gameplay loop experience. The shared upgrade system can feel limiting or in online matches purposefully unfair or targeted, although I play with my dedicated DRG group and we have yet to experience that as friends playing in a private lobby. I think some of the upgrades could be tweaked to feel more impactful, as I feel it took me a good while to find what was and was not working i my builds. I think the timer needs to be longer and the decisions you make should feel more impactful. Many critical reviews are like this and provide good and informative constructive feedback for the devs.

With those criticisms in acknowledged and with a good few I can say I greed with, those points are often not what I have seen in a lot of reviews. I have seen sexist comments about the fact that the game includes women, which is crazy and kinda embarrassing that we are seeing that as a perceived negative in 2026. I have seen review bombers being rude or outright hateful towards the developers at times. There is a degree of vitriol and hatred that is frankly undeserved and goes beyond constructive and ventures into hate and harassment. To those people, you should be ashamed. If you have spewed hateful rhetoric or attacked members of the community or the dev team online, you give the rest of us a bad name. A bunch of Leaf Lovers.

Conclusion:
If it doesn't appeal to you right now, that's fine. It could use some refinement to really reach its full potential. This new take may not be for everyone. I still highly encourage people to give it a shot. I hope despite the flaws that you will love it as much as I do! I look forward to seeing how the game grows and improves in future updates!

As a DRG veteran with prior experience in rogue-likes and modded DRG, I enjoy this game overall. I am excited to watch the game slowly make it to its 1.0 release. That being said, there are definitely a few things that need polish, and I can understand why the reviews are mixed at this point in time.

Rogue Core is a much more tense and stressful game than its predecessor. While the Reclaimer’s Handbook and Tutorial do their job at introducing you to the basics of the game, new players can still be discouraged by Rogue Core’s difficulty/learning curve. The developers previously equated Depth 1 to being like DRG’s Hazard 3. Even with prior DRG experience, there is a chance that you won’t win your first run, as you will still have to adjust to the game’s mechanics. For example, you could be in a room full of Expenite, an Event, a Bio Booster, and a Workbench and STILL have to walk away from the majority of it due to sheer swarm pressure and the ticking timer. That is part of the game, as you will be punished heavily for taking your time and overstaying, especially due to the Reaper Worms that can remove you from the current stage until you are rescued in the next one (in solo you just fail). In comparison, in DRG, most missions allow you to clear out the entire cave at your own pace (excluding a few Hazard 5 missions) and get all the loot.

While it can certainly be expanded on as the game moves toward 1.0, I still enjoy the buildcrafting in Rogue Core, as it still allows you to create broken builds with good synergies. You can create builds that delete the Gatekeepers’ health with one shot, chain elemental effects to all the surrounding enemies that stunlocks them and deals massive damage, become a temp shock machine while regaining ability charge after every enemy killed, etc. That being said, it is definitely harder than in other Rogue-likes to get a “stupidly OP broken build” that I feel most people in this game want to feel the satisfaction of obtaining. It does not help that sometimes all a Workbench will offer you is a new crappy weapon, subpar weapon upgrades, and ability upgrades you do not really need but, ultimately, end up being the better choice anyway. The fact that you can only pick one option from the Workbench also limits buildcrafting, especially if the inverse of what I said happens to be true (super good weapon option, useful weapon upgrades, etc.). Add all this onto the fact that, due to timer pressure, you might be forced to skip certain things that could make your build stronger, including Expenite veins and events to obtain Expenite upgrades. Most people probably feel a degree of dissatisfaction because of this, especially since the game gives you less chances to really “savor” your build since you will be punished for overstaying.

I enjoy playing all the classes and each one can be successful in my opinion. Even Spotter, whose role is more support oriented, can create really good synergies with boosted crit and has the ability to spot Cave Leeches and other enemies on the roof. Falconer, especially with the right Bio Boosters, can deal a lot of electric damage for crowd control and have high uptime with her Falcon. Retcon can be stupid broken and can be clutch in difficult situations. Guardian can stunlock the boss, provide armor for his teammates, and does extremely well in providing space for revives, repairing the elevator drive, etc. Slicer is highly mobile and is extremely strong once melee upgrades start stacking. The gunplay, especially with some of the new weapons, feels great. 

In terms of matchmaking, soloing with Cooper does have a learning curve to it. While Cooper is there to help you mine, carry stuff, and revive you if you make a mistake, you still have to juggle multiple tasks at once, with some Expenite events being an automatic skip for me since they carry a lot of risk to them. Even one of my friends, who has thousands of hours in DRG, is still adjusting to the amount of task management required for a solo D2. Soloing without Cooper is possible, but the game is definitely not balanced around that. Co-op/public lobbies can often be chaotic and unforgiving, especially on higher difficulties. One player falling behind or getting downed affects everyone, especially if you have to rescue them from the Reaper Worm cocoon. The cocoon spawns in a swarm to apply pressure onto you, resulting in a potentially uphill battle that, even if won, will still leave you “behind pace”” and force you to rush to the elevator due to the timer. Despite this, from my experiences, the community still maintains that “high trust” from DRG, where most people will respect the heart system.

While you will still be rewarded for failed runs, if the Host disconnects/crashes, you will get no tangible rewards. DRG has a system that gives partial rewards if this happens, so I hope Rogue Core adds a feature like this soon. The Reaper Worms can sometimes be glitchy and sometimes it’s often not clear right away if another player got grabbed by one until it’s too late. Plenty of other issues exist, but, based on the fixes in the latest patch, the developers just need time to cook.

If it was not evident already, Rogue Core is much less cozy, casual, and laid back than DRG is. Instead of a chill experience mining, dancing, and drinking together, you either survive together or die together. You and the rest of the Reclaimers can easily die from just a handful of mistakes. However, this does not mean camaraderie does not exist. You and your fellow dwarves can lift together to contribute to opening Omega’s Bar for beer, and you will be incentivized to fight as hard as you can against overwhelming odds for your brothers and sisters. Funny dwarf voicelines still exist, such as when you fall and your dwarf screams “Keeps happeningggggggggggggggg!!!!”

The soundtrack/OST fits the atmosphere really well and is often hype. Even if I am a bit tired from the current run and previous attempts, the boss OST crescendoing and Omega saying “Strike the killing blow, victory is within reach” Warhammer 40K style is an experience in itself. Plunge to Perdition never fails to energize me and keep me going.

Overall I recommend Rogue Core, but not because it is simply “DRG 2.” It is a harsher, spicier, and more stressful experience with a lot of potential in its current Early Access state. However, the same reasons why I like the game may also be the reasons why many players are staying away from it right now.

I have nearly 1000 in OG DRG. Read the reviews, watched videos surrounding the criticism around the timer, shared upgrade pool, and ammo economy. In spite of it I give this entry a thumbs up.

Reasons below:

This is NOT DRG. Best way to describe it as NightReign to Elden Ring. Some of the criticism seems to delve into the hypothetical and some valid.

SHARED UPGRADES: I've had nothing but cooperation with squad mates in public lobbies in upgrade selection, no griefing or BM experienced yet. If you read the reviews you'd be shy in trying to play in pub lobbies, I did, but it was unfounded. And hardly anyone is on mics, be brave and at least call out things to make more use of the time allotted.

There is a certain level of enjoyment of not only getting my build up and running, but to help out the squad mates (the give and take). It would be nice to be reminded the class others are playing & their current perk loadout to best synergize with the team. Spotter players usually spec into crit builds, Slicer melee, etc. 
It's a time waste (more about below) for everyone to have to run to Ellis to initiate the perk draft. Would be better if there was a pop up where everyone clicks to accept to begin the draft, or at minimum a mandatory draft for available perks once in the elevator. 

TIMER: To do away with the timer is the wrong direction to take. It provides that friction between risk/reward, fear/greed that with time can help you prioritize what to focus on and what to skip depending on the mission state. If there was no timer, then everyone would just max scour the map (like I do in OG DRG) for every morsel and the run would go for hours with all the reward and no risk.

I would like to see an increase in the timer overall because of the time waste trying to corral people to Ellis to perk draft (that should be changed) or other things that the full squad must be there for. Creates a hurry up and wait feeling. That and the random mini waves eats up time too.

I find it unfair that you can start the extract and the worms will still spawn if it spills over to the "out of time" segment. Perhaps it would be better to cancel the worms from showing if started before timer runs out. Maybe make the extract waves harder the closer you start towards the end to a cap - would play into the risk/reward a bit more fairly imo. 

AMMO ECONOMY: In my opening hours I felt the lack of ammo the most, but more playtime and it's become less of an issue. Some characters are very ammo efficient (Retcon) and some guns are more than others and the less efficient guns can be offset with Spotter's extra resupply ability. 

There are 3 resupplies per level, and I would agree that perhaps they should hold up to 8 ammo packs or increase the ammo pool of the weapons.

The lack of ammo is most apparent in the "Double Enemy Health" alteration that can accompany a run for added difficulty. I've attempted many times and have never been able to successfully complete a run. Especially if you try to release the Expenite Crassis - it's health pool is ungodly. 

GUNPLAY: This is a combat focused version of the DRG universe and most of the weapons feel good to use. If you took the reviews at face value you'd think the new guns are trash, far from the truth. There are only a couple guns I can think of that likely need tweaks. Since it's combat focused, the mobs clipping through the floor/grates is a problem no unfamiliar with OG DRG - but it's a bigger issue here due to the focus of the game. And the big spawn that shoots a death laser at you doesn't have sound ques, insta down you and anyone caught in its path, and goes through terrain - this obviously needs fixing. 

Overall this is an early access game but any early access will be judged since it is playable now. People forget how bare bones OG DRG was and comparing EA states is a night/day difference between the two.

There is fun to be had in this game if you're someone who enjoys a faster-paced experience with a foundation of systems that will likely get ironed out and tuned during EA.

I read a few negative reviews. Boy this game does NOT deserve them, this is kind of disrespectful for me to say, but I feel like I'm watching toddlers complain that the royal palace they just moved into is slightly different. We would NOT have liked a game that was exactly like DRG, that's what DRG is for.

It's much more polished than DRG was upon Early Access and is already a blast to play. It's sorta like if you took Deep Rock Galactic, allowing silly powerful builds that Hades has, and made it less about hanging out in a cave doing all the cave things and instead blasting through hordes vermintide-style barely making it out alive. Also while sporting some crazy new abilities.

Let me hit on every negative point, and tell you why its actually a positive. For reference, I play this game on max difficulty and am 20 hours in. I played after their initial balancing patch addressing timer and ammo:

UPGRADES SUCKING? I fully expected boring upgrades, played many games with them where designers were too afraid to give players power, but I was surprised to find out each upgrade you get in a run is quite meaty and noticeable, and best of all can STACK. for instance, a gun can get 50% rebound chance. Stack it again and it turns a pistol into a horde clearing gun.

ASSET FLIP? Yes and no. I was pleasantly surprised by the fact the game features a lot of new weapons custom built for the game, with some classic DRG weapons making a reappearance. The games entire aesthetic is a lot more sleek, techy, and serious, matching the seriousness of the reclaimers as they take on a deadly mission. The UI is completely new, the lobby is new, they music is new, the classes are new, there are new abilities, all new enemies, and the game loop is far different, yada yada.

SOME CLASSES SUCK: hard disagree. Any new class feels sucky at first, give it some time, they all have strengths.

SHARING UPGRADES: Yeah it sucks with malicious teammates, but most are not like that. I kinda like the social dynamic of everyone looking over a selection of upgrades together and parcelling them out, you can see how people are building themselves alongside you. They took a risk doing this, since most games remove any and all friction of social interaction, but when they lean into the friction, it can make playing with others a much more beautiful experience.

AMMO RUNNING OUT? Honestly, this happens in DRG all the time, this is NOT new. It's a threat that needs to be present, asking players to get smarter with how weapons get used. The game also gives dwarves more ways of dealing damage outside of guns. Melee is stronger. recharging class abilities sometimes deal significant damage.

RNG? I've heard people complain you HAVE to have the platform gun, or HAVE to have a red sugar upgrade, etc.. My experience is most of my difficulty in the game was simply not knowing how to play it yet... some runs can feel heavier than others, but there are many many ways to skin this cat that at least one dwarf on your team is going to turn into a monster shredding monster. If the game was evened out so you always gain a certain amount of power, the tradeoff is that the designers are taking away those moments when you experience a high of power after not quite figuring out a previous run.

ARMOR SUCKS? so instead of a recharging shield you have "armor", a second health bar. I believe the devs made the right call making it operate like health. It asks you to build around either around planning on taking damage (and bringing back armor through goofy means), or avoiding damage altogether with fast kills or fast movement. Perks often play with the idea of always being low on armor, or always being topped off. its spicy. Its interesting. A recharging shield evens out the experience, taking away the diversity of builds.

THE TIMER: yeah so in DRG people tend to extract every goody out of a cave, do every event, etc.. in Deep Core there is a timer spelling impending doom, summon horrifying tentacles to drag your team into the depths. You can fight them off, but its legit bad news. Its kinda awesome. It turns the game into a delicate balance of trying to milk a cave for all its upgrades, and remembering you actually wanna stay alive. It forces your team to keep a move on. I hope the devs do not nerf it further as it has been balanced just right. This is a game about resource management.

YOU CAN DIE, AND WILL DIE A LOT: I dunno what players expected, yeah? Its not much of a rogue like if its easy to master. Your supposed to die, learn, try and get a bit farther, rinse and repeat. I find this game, after an initial "holy crap this is hard" period is much more merciful than a title like Hades.

My only real complaint with the game, and with DRG as well, is the UI/UX is far from elegant, with information changing positions per screen and it being difficult to digest what is going on with your build mid-mission at a glance. I really don't like that cosmetics are unlocked per class. The world of Deep Rock has so many beards and hats that this type of padding doesn't need to exist.

I love the gym. I love the new mission control. Love the gauntlet abilites, love re-experiencing the tension DRG use to hold for me.

Anyways, I recommend it 100000%. Did not regret buying early. Keep it up Ghost Ship!

In the original, getting dead drunk and dancing before a mission, or shouting “we’re rich” at a chunk of gold until Mission Control got a headache, made perfect sense because the dwarves were reckless miners in a corporate deathtrap. In Rogue Core, the Reclaimers are supposed to be more serious and elite, so those same rituals feel strangely out of place.

The best example is the new workout system. Workouts could be a great way to give mission buffs, like the special beers in DRG. But making me play a repetitive minigame just to order a round for my colleagues is annoying and kills the fun. I know Rogue Core is not DRG, and the gameplay can change of course. Deep Rock Galactic: Rogue Core Review — The Brilliant (and Frustrating) Dilemma of the Roguelike Dwarf

Lately everyone is debating the upgrade systems, the brutal difficulty, and how well Ghost Ship Games’ formula adapts to a roguelike loop and honestly, Ghost Ship Games are absolute legends; their track record proves they make games with genuine passion and quality. However, as with any new experimental venture in the industry, sometimes you have to screw up a bit before you can reach heaven. In my time with Rogue Core, I’ve noticed a massive design flaw in its opening hours that nobody is talking about, and it’s time to put it on the table.

The Gauntlet Mode and the Design Paradox

Let’s first talk about what works spectacularly well: Gauntlet mode. If you check the forums or talk to the community, the vast majority agrees that playing a Gauntlet run is when you truly experience the game Rogue Core was actually built for. That’s where the formula explodes, the synergies click, and your dwarf feels like a true mining and killing machine.

But here lies the grand paradox and, honestly, it’s a tragedy when a studio designs a game with such a brilliant vision for its endgame, yet the barrier to entry in the first few hours is so flawed that many players will get frustrated way too early. A lot of people will throw in the towel and never get to experience the game at its maximum potential.


The Frustration of the First Workbench

Where does this frustration come from? It happens in the initial runs (those 3 levels + 1 boss level format). In their eagerness to deliver a pure, hardcore roguelike experience, the game commits a major tactical sin: at the very start of a run, secondary weapons have an incredibly high spawn rate at the workbench.

This is deeply frustrating. That initial burst of excitement and adrenaline you feel when starting a new run completely vanishes the moment you interact with that first workbench and see nothing but secondary weapons or short-range shotguns. Being forced to start a run with a weapon that doesn't help you in the early game—and actually actively hinders you—adds an artificial difficulty barrier. I am certain this wasn't the intended experience Ghost Ship Games had in mind when they coded this.

The solution is logical and clean: secondary weapons should be completely removed from the initial selection pool. Players should always start with a solid primary weapon option (except heavy choices). Later in the run, if they decide they want a secondary, they can make that strategic choice at advanced workbenches.

Furthermore, there’s a noticeable lack of freshness in the starting arsenal. It feels like they dropped the ball on creating more unique primary weapons and grenades with perks designed specifically for this new experience, rather than just copying and pasting so much content from the original game.

The Isaac vs. Satan Syndrome: A Pacing Issue

To understand why these short, initial runs feel so bad, we can use a perfect analogy: it’s like if The Binding of Isaac forced you to fight Satan after clearing only 3 or 4 floors of farming. You simply don't have the space or the time to piece together a proper build. Because you have so few floors to upgrade and evolve your dwarf, the boss battle at the end of these starter runs feels unfair and hollow—an incomplete experience compared to the wonderful balance found in Gauntlet mode.

Conclusion: Adjust the Perspective, don`t touch the numbers, yet...

This critique doesn't come from a place of hate, but from a desire to see Rogue Core shine the way it deserves to. I firmly believe that not everything in video games is fixed by simply tweaking numbers or scaling enemy damage up and down. In this case, the game's flow is tripping over itself right at the starting line.

The solution isn't that complex: it's about shifting the mindset and understanding that in a short 3 to 4-level run, the player needs to feel like they can "break the game." If we aren't getting more floors to farm, then give us double the rewards. A great fix would be that in these short, non-Gauntlet runs, every time we level up our XP or hit a workbench, we get double the upgrades or perks. This way, Gauntlet mode can maintain its current neutral strategic pacing, while the shorter runs become fast, chaotic, and deeply satisfying power-trips.

Small design adjustments like these will make a world of difference. It’s just a matter of adapting their perspective to this risky new genre mashup. The foundation for another masterpiece is right there; now it’s up to Ghost Ship Games to polish the gem. Rock and Stone!

rogue core in its current state is very flawed but still very fun. prepare for a short list of pros and cons

pros:

-incredibly satisfying gunplay, most weapons are capable of being more fun than anything in base DRG if you ask me. this includes weapons that actually are from base DRG because of workbench upgrades and build synergy

-arguably high general difficulty. I consider this a pro because it keeps the game from feeling too easy and makes busted builds feel more rewarding

-classes feel distinct and fun to play similar to base DRG. the class abilities go a long way since you can upgrade them through various means

-solid gameplay loop. do as many tasks as you can during calm periods, choose to fight during swarms, continue doing tasks, or try doing both. reach the boss fight, win or lose, and do it again. I think there’s enough variety and familiarity to keep things fun

cons:

-the co-op experience isn’t great right now. I’ve had much more fun doing solo runs where you don’t have to wait for others to come to a zone that *requires* all players to be present. I don’t mind the negotiation system itself but it’s the way you access it that’s annoying more often than not, and this of course extends to anything else that requires players in a zone

-the negotiation system. I did say I don’t mind its current implementation, but it could certainly be made better and more fair for everyone. other reviewers have already had some good ideas for how to improve it so I won’t try to come up with my own, but rerolls and card flips would be a great start

-frustrating gameplay changes, a main one for me being the slowdown when falling from a certain height. this mechanic wasn’t in base DRG so I have no idea why they decided to add it to this faster-paced more intense version… another annoying change is the armor system instead of DRG’s regenerating energy shield. armor is plentiful in this game but that doesn’t really matter when it feels like it barely helps and gets depleted in 2 seconds. then you have to find an armor source or hope to find an upgrade that gives you armor in some way

I do definitely recommend the game despite its problems which will hopefully be solved over time. the foundation they have here is super strong and I believe it will shape up to be a great game. if you’re on the fence about getting it, just be aware that you might be frustrated and disappointed in many ways and you might want to check back later when development has progressed. if you’re looking for a fun and intense solo experience though, I think you should try it

As a long time fan of the original DRG, but also of rogue-likes, my main takeaway here is this brings the lesser elements of each, rather than drawing on their strengths. 
- The level layouts are fairly prescriptive and repetitive, which lends itself to a very samey feel, unlike DRG. 
- The builds available feel either poorly balanced, or limited in their scope, which encourages players to shoot for familiar safe builds rather than experiment in the manner of a rogue like. 
- A significant number of potential weapon options are so poor as to immediately compromise a run from the outset in solo, or lead to a massive power imbalance in groups. 
- The frequency and style of enemy encounters mean you WILL take chip damage by the wave, which means certain healing powerups become essentially mandatory picks, but the scaling means that once you have them, damage is almost meaningless.
- Very limited enemy variation, combined with the limited maps mean that almost every fight feels the same.
- The negotiation system on upgrades means that build variety in groups is extremely hit or miss, with typically one or two players of the group getting synergisticaly interesting options, and the rest of the group being left with very generic choices.

I really want to recommend this game, but as things currently stand, feedback and suggestions from the numerous beta testing phases do not seem to have been taken on board, and it comes at a hefty price point for what it offers. If it were ~40% cheaper, or offered more long term playability I would recommend it, but currently I cannot. If you're new and looking for a roguelike shooter with good variety, check out Roboquest or Risk of Rain.

Connecting to a random lobby - you won't easily find this coordination, resulting in frustrating waiting periods that often end the run.

My reccomendations that would instantly improve most of the experience for me:
-Most upgrades should be easier to start (maybe something like being able to choose upgrades on your own as they become available, or maybe start the upgrade phase based on a vote rather than gathering in an area)
-More than one of a class should be allowed (at least make it an option to toggle for the host like DRG)
-Events requiring all players in an area should be relaxed a bit on easier difficulties.
-Some PC performance optimization is needed.

Overall I'd fully reccomend this game if you have friends to play it with. But the current solo experience can be a bit mixed depending on what type of lobbies you connect to.
